quote: I feel reasonably confident in venturing that Aumann must, at one point or another, have questioned his faith. And yet he did not doubt successfully.
content: The Hart interview should have been read and quoted. Fable's criticism of the essay's guessing is fair. But what Aumann says there, that religion and science are separate spheres and that he does not hold his faith as a hypothesis that competes with evidence (Hart 2005), is an eloquent version of the outcome the essay describes. Book I names that move: "The dragon is in a separate magisterium." A Bayesian whose theorem says honest reasoners cannot agree to disagree has put one domain outside its reach. That is not a refutation of the essay's claim. It is what not doubting successfully looks like from the inside. The essay's warning concerns what the fortress looks like to the person who lives in it, and a lucid statement of the two-spheres view does not answer it.

quote: Many in this world retain beliefs whose flaws a ten-year-old could point out, if that ten-year-old were hearing the beliefs for the first time.
content: Kelemen's teleology is about rocks and animals having purposes. It is not about particular doctrines, and the ten-year-old in the essay is hearing "the beliefs for the first time": a talking snake, a parted sea, a virgin birth. That case has been tested. Children from secular homes classified the protagonists of stories with miraculous events as fictional, while children from religious homes judged them real, and the difference tracked religious exposure, not age (Corriveau, Chen & Harris 2015). A child with no religious upbringing handles miracle stories the way the essay says, as fiction. A general bias toward purpose is not the same thing as a readiness to believe particular claims. The essay's witness exists and has been measured.

quote: On my more pessimistic days I wonder if the camel has two humps.
content: Here Fable is right. Bornat retracted the "camel has two humps" claim in 2014, and the line should carry an "oops." It was published as a musing ("On my more pessimistic days I wonder"), and the retraction came six years after the essay. The essay's argument does not need it. The instruction that follows, to stop your mind from completing the pattern even when the pattern is "Occam's Razor!", holds whether or not the audience's difficulty with meta-level arguments is innate. Fable's note fits the essay's own subject, which is updating when your source turns out to be bad.
